title: Bharmaur: the homeland of the Gaddis
body: Bharmaur tribal area comprises the Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh and has been a notified tribal area since 21 November 1975. It is inhabited by the Gaddis, a tribal community who practised transhumance and speak the Gaddiali dialect. The region has a harsh climate, a low resource base and a fragile environment. Under the Fifth Five Year Plan, the tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 and Bharmaur became one of five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in the state. The plan gave the highest priority to transport and communications, agriculture and allied activities, and social and community services. Schools, healthcare, potable water, roads and electricity were developed, but villages along the river Ravi in the Holi and Khani areas benefited most, while remote villages in the Tundah and Kugti areas still lack sufficient infrastructure. Female literacy rose from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011, the sex ratio improved and child marriage declined. Cultivation of pulses and cash crops increased, though with traditional technology. Only about one-tenth of households now practise transhumance, yet many Gaddis migrate to Kangra in winter to earn a living from wage labour.

title: Indira Gandhi Canal command area
body: The Indira Gandhi Canal, earlier called the Rajasthan Canal, was launched on 31 March 1958. It originates at the Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to the Pakistan border in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan. Its planned length is 9,060 km and its total culturable command area is 19.63 lakh hectares. Stage-I (Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern Bikaner) has a culturable command area of 5.53 lakh hectares and got irrigation in the early 1960s. Stage-II (Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu), with shifting sand dunes and summer temperatures near 50 degrees Celsius, covers 14.10 lakh hectares and began receiving irrigation in the mid-1980s. Longer availability of soil moisture, afforestation and pasture development have greened the land and reduced wind erosion and siltation of canals. Cultivated area and cropping intensity increased, and the traditional crops gram, bajra and jowar were replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice. However, intensive irrigation and excessive use of water have led to waterlogging and soil salinity.
